content: {"id": "967f1894-393c-4cf9-a8e3-7164083d9b8b", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "My AWS Config setup has two conformance packs - a NIST 800-53 pack and a PCI DSS pack - that share about 40% of their rules. Separate auditors consume the NIST compliance report and the PCI compliance report independently. To cut Config evaluation costs, should I merge them into one combined conformance pack? Explain the tradeoff. No account access required.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
{"id": "62abad16-63fd-44e3-b7a5-c45fceb0d621", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "chat_title", "title": "AWS Config conformance pack consolidation cost tradeoff analysis"}]}

{"id": "6eea9edd-2a0d-449f-8f45-640be9de6b10", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Short answer: merging won't actually save you money, and it will cost you the clean separation your auditors rely on. Here's why.

**Why merging doesn't reduce evaluation costs**

AWS Config charges per configuration item recorded and per rule evaluation, based on unique *rule instances* — not per conformance pack. If a rule (say, `RESTRICTED_SSH`) appears in both packs today, deploying it via two separate conformance packs typically means AWS Config creates two separately-managed rule instances, each evaluating independently. When you merge into one pack, the overlapping 40% collapses down to a single rule instance each — so you *do* cut redundant evaluations for that shared 40%, roughly proportional to the overlap.

But that saving is available **without merging the packs**, by simply deconstructing the overlap: identify the ~40% of rules that are identical (same rule, same parameters) across both packs, and deploy those once, in a shared/base conformance pack, while keeping the NIST-only and PCI-only rules in their own thin packs layered on top. That gets you the same cost reduction as a full merge, because the cost driver is duplicate rule evaluation, not the number of packs.

**The tradeoff if you fully merge into one pack**

| | Two packs (or base + 2 thin packs) | One fully merged pack |
|---|---|---|
| Evaluation cost | Same low cost once overlap is deduplicated | Same low cost |
| Auditor-facing compliance report | Clean, scoped: NIST auditor sees only NIST rules; PCI auditor sees only PCI rules | Single report mixing both frameworks' rules — auditors must filter out irrelevant rules themselves |
| Compliance pack conformance score | Two independent scores, each meaningful to its framework | One blended score that doesn't map cleanly to either framework's pass/fail criteria |
| Maintenance | Update NIST rules without touching PCI pack, and vice versa | Any update risks touching both frameworks' scope; harder to reason about change impact |
| Drift/versioning | Each framework can version independently (e.g., PCI DSS 4.0 update doesn't touch NIST pack) | Framework updates get entangled in one artifact |

**Recommendation**

Don't do a full merge. Instead:

1. Extract the ~40% overlapping rules into a shared base conformance pack (deployed once).
2. Keep two thin, framework-specific conformance packs on top containing only the rules unique to NIST and unique to PCI respectively.
3. Each auditor still gets a report scoped to their framework — you just point them at "base pack + NIST pack" or "base pack + PCI pack" results combined (most audit tooling can already aggregate multiple packs' rule results per resource).

This gets you the full cost benefit of deduplication while preserving the separate, auditor-friendly compliance reports you need. A true single merged pack saves you nothing further on cost but does real damage to reporting clarity.

If you want, I can walk through how to identify exactly which rules overlap and check current evaluation volume — that would need to look at your actual Config setup though. Want me to dig into your account?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
